title: Punna goes west
hookLine: to a fierce land: if they insult me, I'll think them kind for not hitting me

cards: A new job, a new city, a team with a reputation. Everyone warns you: they're rough over there. You'll get eaten alive.
The hundred and forty-fifth discourse starts with a monk named Punna asking the Buddha for a short teaching before he leaves. The Buddha gives it, then asks: where will you live?
Punna names a region to the west called Sunaparanta. The Buddha says, plainly: the people there are fierce, Punna. They're rough.
What will you do if they insult you?

teach.b: The short teaching comes first. If you delight in what you see, hear, smell, taste, touch and think, and hold on to it, suffering comes. If you don't, it ends.
Then the conversation, like a ladder going down.
If they insult you? Punna: I'll think, these people are good, really good, since they don't hit me with their fists. And if they hit you?
At least they don't throw clods of earth at me. And if they do? At least they don't beat me with a stick.
And if they do? At least they don't use a knife.
The Buddha keeps going, all the way to the worst, and Punna's answer never turns to hate. Even facing the end of his life, he answers calmly. Good, Punna, the Buddha says.
With such self-control and peace, you can live there. Punna goes.

The text says that in that one rains retreat he brought around five hundred men and five hundred women as lay followers, realized the three knowledges, and later attained final release. A word of care, though.
This is a monk's training in patience, chosen freely, in a teaching about not clinging.

teach.h: NOT ADVICE TO STAY IN HARM
teach.b: It isn't advice to stay where someone hurts you. What anyone can borrow is the move itself: when something sharp lands, notice what didn't happen.
They were rude, but they didn't shout. The email was curt, but it wasn't cruel. That's not pretending it was fine.
It's refusing to let the worst version take over the mind.

how: Punna's answers are taught as an example of patience (khanti), which Theravada counts among the perfections (parami) a practitioner develops.

o: silently accepting any harm done to you
a monk's journey to a distant land
patience, bearing hard things without hatred

p: at least not hit with fists
at least not clods of earth
the fierce land to the west

s: the Buddha tells Punna the people of Sunaparanta are gentle
he warns him they are fierce and rough.
Punna's answers never turn to hatred, even at the worst
at each step he finds something that didn't happen, and stays calm.
the story is advice to stay in a harmful situation
it's a monk's freely chosen training in patience, not a rule for anyone being hurt.

games.q: you're Punna. the Buddha asks: what if they hit you with their fists? what do you answer?
o: they're good people, since they don't throw clods of earth at me.
games.why: at every step down the ladder, Punna finds the harm that didn't happen, and the Buddha says he is ready to live there.

practice: Bring to mind a small sting from recently, a curt reply, an eye-roll, a comment that landed: not a deep wound, just a small one, and notice how it sits in the body.
Then try Punna's step and ask what didn't happen: they were short with me, but they didn't. Let the sting be its real size, no bigger, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Khanti. Patience, forbearance: Punna, a monk heading to a fierce land, answers every imagined harm without hatred, at least they didn't do worse. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali khanti: patience, forbearance. Punna's answers are taught as an example of it.

carryVoice: Your line: at least they didn't. Patience here means seeing a hurt at its real size, never staying where you're harmed. Day five hundred ten.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 145, Punnovada Sutta (advice to Punna)
